questions.question: In an idealized LV pressure–volume experiment, end-diastolic volume increases while arterial afterload and contractile state are held constant. Which change is expected?
options: A wider loop with a steeper end-systolic relationship
A wider loop with increased stroke volume along an unchanged end-systolic relationship
A narrower loop with increased end-systolic volume
A leftward shift of the diastolic pressure–volume relationship
questions.explanation:
Preload and the Frank–Starling Response

Correct answer: A wider loop with increased stroke volume along an unchanged end-systolic relationship

Distinguish Loading From Contractile State

**Preload is the myocardial stretch before contraction**, commonly approximated by end-diastolic volume in an idealized loop. More filling can increase ejection through the Frank–Starling mechanism.

Stroke volume is end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume and corresponds to loop width. The end-systolic relationship need not become steeper for stroke volume to increase.

End-diastolic pressure is not interchangeable with volume: compliance and external restraint influence the pressure produced by a given volume.

Apply the Model With Clinical Qualifications

**A larger stroke volume does not independently demonstrate improved intrinsic contractility.** Compare loading conditions before interpreting serial measurements.

The idealized experiment fixes variables that often change together in patients. A fluid bolus can alter arterial pressure, ventricular interaction and valve regurgitation as well as filling.

Use the model to explain a physiologic response, not to justify fluid administration to every hypotensive patient. Assess congestion, perfusion and the specific cause of instability. Fluid responsiveness describes a potential rise in output with additional preload; it does not establish that fluid is necessary or that its benefits exceed the risk of pulmonary or systemic congestion. A high filling pressure can coexist with poor forward flow and should not be interpreted as evidence that another bolus will help.

A wider loop with a steeper end-systolic relationship: A steeper end-systolic pressure–volume relationship indicates increased contractile state, whereas the experiment specifies unchanged contractility despite the larger stroke volume.

A narrower loop with increased end-systolic volume: This pattern fits an acute increase in afterload or reduced contractility more closely; an isolated preload increase normally augments stroke volume through length-dependent activation.

A leftward shift of the diastolic pressure–volume relationship: An altered diastolic relationship indicates a change in chamber filling properties; increasing filling volume moves the operating point along the existing relationship rather than proving changed compliance.

questions.question: At fixed initial LV end-diastolic volume, arterial pressure is abruptly increased. The first pressure–volume loop is taller and narrower, with greater end-systolic volume; its end-systolic point remains on the original end-systolic relationship. Which interpretation is best?
options: Increased preload with unchanged afterload
Reduced contractility with unchanged afterload
Increased afterload with preserved contractile state
Reduced diastolic compliance with unchanged afterload
questions.explanation:
Afterload Versus Reduced Contractility

Correct answer: Increased afterload with preserved contractile state

Identify the Variable That Changed

**Afterload is the load opposing myocardial shortening.** In this experiment the ventricle ejects against a higher arterial pressure, leaving more volume at end systole.

With the initial filling volume fixed, a higher residual end-systolic volume means a smaller stroke volume and lower ejection fraction on that beat.

A fall in EF therefore does not by itself prove that intrinsic contractility deteriorated. Clinical afterload also depends on arterial impedance and ventricular geometry, not only a cuff pressure.

Use End-Systolic Behavior to Clarify Mechanism

**The end-systolic pressure–volume relationship helps distinguish load change from contractile-state change.** Its slope is often called end-systolic elastance.

Reduced contractile state shifts the relation downward/rightward; increased contractile state generally shifts it upward/leftward. Interpretation ideally uses a family of loops across changing loads.

The relationship is relatively load insensitive within a useful range, not perfectly independent of all physiology. Do not infer a measured elastance from a single routine echo EF. In clinical assessment, combine pressure, chamber size, valve disease and the treatment context. Subsequent beats can develop secondary preload changes as residual volume accumulates, which is why this stem specifies the first beat and fixed initial end-diastolic volume.

Increased preload with unchanged afterload: Additional preload increases starting end-diastolic volume and usually broadens the loop under otherwise fixed conditions; the stem fixes initial filling volume and raises arterial pressure.

Reduced contractility with unchanged afterload: Reduced contractility shifts the end-systolic relationship downward and rightward; the preserved relationship and higher arterial load instead support a loading effect.

Reduced diastolic compliance with unchanged afterload: Reduced compliance alters the diastolic pressure–volume relationship and filling pressure; it does not explain the stated acute arterial load and preserved end-systolic relationship.

questions.question: Two ventricles have the same end-diastolic volume, but one requires a substantially higher end-diastolic pressure. Its end-diastolic pressure–volume curve lies upward and leftward. Which property is reduced?
options: End-systolic elastance
Diastolic chamber compliance
Effective arterial elastance
End-diastolic chamber stiffness
questions.explanation:
Ventricular Compliance and Filling Pressure

Correct answer: Diastolic chamber compliance

Relate Pressure Change to Volume Change

**Compliance is the change in volume divided by the corresponding change in pressure**, evaluated over the relevant portion of the filling curve. Stiffness is its reciprocal.

A less compliant ventricle develops greater pressure for a comparable volume. Because the diastolic curve is nonlinear, its local slope changes as filling increases.

A high filling pressure is therefore not a direct measurement of an excessive end-diastolic volume. Hypertrophy and fibrosis are potential contributors, while pericardial restraint and ventricular interaction can affect chamber behavior.

Keep Relaxation, Compliance and EF Separate

**Active relaxation and passive filling properties are related but different components of diastolic function.** Impaired relaxation affects early filling; chamber stiffness affects the pressure–volume relationship.

Preserved EF describes the proportion of end-diastolic volume ejected and does not establish normal filling pressures or exclude a heart-failure syndrome.

Clinical evaluation requires symptoms, signs and appropriate objective evidence rather than diagnosing HFpEF from one pressure or a normal EF alone. Interpret Doppler findings in their rhythm and loading context and consider external restraint when pressures and volumes appear discordant. Treatment should address the actual cause of congestion and impaired function; the curve alone does not select a drug or establish that more fluid will improve output.

End-systolic elastance: End-systolic elastance characterizes systolic pressure–volume behavior and contractile state; the stated curve is an end-diastolic filling relationship.

Effective arterial elastance: Effective arterial elastance summarizes aspects of arterial load, usually from end-systolic pressure relative to stroke volume, rather than the ventricular diastolic filling curve.

End-diastolic chamber stiffness: Stiffness is the reciprocal of compliance; higher pressure for the same volume indicates increased rather than reduced stiffness.

questions.question: In the conventional LV pressure–volume model with competent valves, which pressure configuration occurs during isovolumetric relaxation before mitral opening?
options: Aortic pressure exceeds LV pressure, and left atrial pressure exceeds LV pressure
LV pressure exceeds both aortic and left atrial pressure
Aortic pressure exceeds LV pressure, and LV pressure still exceeds left atrial pressure
LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure, and left atrial pressure exceeds LV pressure
questions.explanation:
Valve Timing and Isovolumetric Relaxation

Correct answer: Aortic pressure exceeds LV pressure, and LV pressure still exceeds left atrial pressure

Follow the Pressure Crossings

**Isovolumetric relaxation lies between aortic closure and mitral opening in the conventional model.** LV pressure falls while both valves remain closed and volume stays approximately at end-systolic volume.

The aortic-to-LV gradient supports aortic closure. The mitral valve remains closed until declining LV pressure falls below left atrial pressure.

The preceding isovolumetric contraction interval occurs after mitral closure and before aortic opening, with rising rather than falling ventricular pressure.

Use the Model Without Confusing Electrical and Mechanical Events

**Valve events follow changing pressure gradients rather than a fixed ECG landmark alone.** The ECG provides timing context but does not directly measure opening pressure.

Important regurgitation disrupts the ideal closed-valve, constant-volume assumptions; a pressure–volume diagram must therefore be interpreted in the context of valve competence.

Relaxation time also depends on loading: a high left atrial pressure can promote earlier mitral opening even when myocardial relaxation is impaired. A short interval does not independently prove normal diastolic function. Distinguish the chamber-level model from the motion of every individual muscle fiber, since constant cavity volume does not require every sarcomere to maintain a fixed length. Clinical Doppler interpretation integrates valve timing, tissue velocities and the pressure context instead of assigning a diagnosis from one interval.

LV phase | Mitral valve | Aortic valve | Volume behavior

Filling | Open | Closed | Increases

Isovolumetric contraction | Closed | Closed | Approximately unchanged

Ejection | Closed | Open | Decreases

Isovolumetric relaxation | Closed | Closed | Approximately unchanged

Aortic pressure exceeds LV pressure, and left atrial pressure exceeds LV pressure: Once left atrial pressure exceeds LV pressure and the mitral valve opens, ventricular filling begins; that is beyond the isovolumetric interval.

LV pressure exceeds both aortic and left atrial pressure: This configuration supports aortic ejection after the outflow valve opens, rather than relaxation with the aortic valve already closed.

LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure, and left atrial pressure exceeds LV pressure: This is not the normal early-diastolic pressure ordering; aortic pressure is higher than LV pressure during the interval following aortic closure.

questions.question: A patient with LV hypertrophy and elevated LV filling pressure develops marked tachycardia without a rise in aortic diastolic pressure. Which mechanism most directly worsens subendocardial oxygen supply–demand balance?
options: Reduced myocardial extraction compensating for increased metabolic demand
A reduced diastolic driving pressure caused by a rise in aortic pressure
Shorter diastolic perfusion time with increased oxygen demand
Longer systolic ejection providing additional subendocardial perfusion
questions.explanation:
Tachycardia and Left Ventricular Supply–Demand Balance

Correct answer: Shorter diastolic perfusion time with increased oxygen demand

Separate Perfusion Time From Driving Pressure

**Left ventricular subendocardial flow is strongly dependent on diastole** because systolic contraction compresses intramyocardial vessels. A higher heart rate shortens available diastolic time.

A useful simplified driving-pressure estimate is aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure. Elevated LV filling pressure reduces that gradient even when systemic arterial pressure appears acceptable.

The estimate is a teaching approximation, not a complete measurement of coronary resistance, phasic flow or microvascular function.

Recognize Simultaneous Demand and Filling Effects

**Tachycardia also increases myocardial oxygen demand.** Hypertrophy can increase vulnerability when coronary flow reserve cannot compensate.

Shorter diastole can impair filling, particularly with impaired relaxation or loss of atrial contribution. The result depends on rhythm, rate, loading and the underlying disease.

Evaluate ischemic symptoms in context rather than assuming either fixed epicardial stenosis or a purely rate-related cause. Correct the precipitant and assess hemodynamic stability before choosing rate or rhythm treatment. This mechanism does not mean that every elevated heart rate should be suppressed: compensatory sinus tachycardia during shock may reflect an unmet circulatory need. Clinical action follows the cause and perfusion assessment, while the physiology explains why uncontrolled tachycardia can become harmful in a vulnerable ventricle.

Reduced myocardial extraction compensating for increased metabolic demand: Increased demand requires more supply or extraction, not a reduction in extraction as a protective response; the myocardium already extracts a substantial fraction of delivered oxygen.

A reduced diastolic driving pressure caused by a rise in aortic pressure: A rise in aortic diastolic pressure would tend to increase the simplified driving gradient if LVEDP were unchanged; no arterial rise is supplied here.

Longer systolic ejection providing additional subendocardial perfusion: LV systolic compression limits subendocardial flow; increased rate does not improve supply by creating a longer favorable systolic perfusion interval.

questions.question: With severe acute RV pressure loading, echocardiography shows RV dilation, leftward septal displacement and a small LV cavity. LV EF is preserved, but systemic output falls. Which mechanism best explains the LV finding?
options: New primary LV contractile failure as the principal cause of low output
LV underfilling from reduced RV delivery and septal/pericardial interaction
Predominantly systemic vasodilation with an incidental RV abnormality
Isolated reduced venous return without mechanical ventricular interaction
questions.explanation:
Ventricular Interdependence in Right Ventricular Loading

Correct answer: LV underfilling from reduced RV delivery and septal/pericardial interaction

Recognize Both Serial and Mechanical Coupling

**Reduced RV forward output limits pulmonary venous return to the LV.** In addition, the ventricles share a septum and are constrained within the pericardial space.

RV dilation and altered transseptal forces can distort LV geometry and reduce filling. These mechanisms can coexist rather than representing competing explanations.

A small, apparently vigorous LV is therefore not reassuring proof of adequate systemic flow. EF is a fraction and can remain normal when absolute stroke volume is low.

Use Loading Assessment to Guide the Next Decision

**Additional fluid is not automatically beneficial in a dilated, pressure-loaded RV.** Excess filling can aggravate septal displacement and congestion.

Assess systemic pressure, congestion, oxygenation, RV perfusion and the cause of elevated afterload. Acute pulmonary embolism, pulmonary vascular disease and ventilator-related loading require different definitive approaches.

Integrate echo with the clinical and hemodynamic picture rather than treating a single chamber measurement as a complete diagnosis. Pressure and volume loading can produce different timing of septal flattening, and mixed disease can blur that distinction. Reassess after intervention: improved arterial pressure alone does not prove restored forward output, just as a lower pulmonary artery pressure can sometimes reflect a failing RV rather than successful unloading.

New primary LV contractile failure as the principal cause of low output: Primary LV dysfunction can lower output, but the small preserved-EF chamber with acute RV dilation and septal shift points to reduced filling rather than demonstrating intrinsic LV failure.

Predominantly systemic vasodilation with an incidental RV abnormality: Vasodilation can lower systemic pressure, but does not explain the stated RV pressure loading, septal displacement and LV underfilling as directly as ventricular interaction.

Isolated reduced venous return without mechanical ventricular interaction: Reduced RV forward delivery is relevant, but leftward septal displacement also provides evidence of mechanical interaction; omitting that component does not fully explain the findings.

questions.question: In isolated mitral regurgitation without a shunt or aortic regurgitation, LV end-diastolic volume is 150 mL and end-systolic volume 50 mL. Correctly measured LVOT forward stroke volume is 55 mL. Which interpretation is correct?
options: LV EF is about 37%, and regurgitant volume is 45 mL per beat
LV EF is about 67%, but regurgitant volume is 45 mL per beat
LV EF is about 67%, and regurgitant volume is 55 mL per beat
LV EF is about 50%, and regurgitant volume is 100 mL per beat
questions.explanation:
Total Versus Forward Stroke Volume in Mitral Regurgitation

Correct answer: LV EF is about 67%, but regurgitant volume is 45 mL per beat

Partition the Ejected Volume

**Total LV stroke volume is EDV minus ESV: 150 − 50 = 100 mL.** Conventional EF is 100/150, approximately 67%.

With isolated MR and the stated exclusions, total ejection separates into forward aortic flow and backward mitral flow. Regurgitant volume is 100 − 55 = 45 mL per beat.

Regurgitant fraction is 45/100, or 45%. Keep its denominator distinct from EDV and from forward stroke volume.

Interpret a Preserved EF in Context

**A preserved conventional EF does not guarantee adequate forward output in regurgitation.** Some of the ejected blood returns to the atrium rather than reaching the systemic circulation.

Integrate valve anatomy, quantitative measurements, ventricular remodeling, symptoms and other supportive findings. One derived value should not independently determine severity or intervention.

These subtraction methods are sensitive to acquisition errors, especially area measurements, and their assumptions fail when additional regurgitant lesions or shunts are present. Verify that measurements refer to comparable beats and loading conditions. A disagreement between measured flows should prompt review of technique before assigning the difference to disease. The distinction also explains why serial EF changes must be interpreted with the loading and valve context rather than equating an apparently high EF with normal intrinsic myocardial performance.

LV EF is about 37%, and regurgitant volume is 45 mL per beat: Dividing forward stroke volume by LV end-diastolic volume gives a forward fraction, not the conventional volume-based LV EF; the latter uses total LV stroke volume.

LV EF is about 67%, and regurgitant volume is 55 mL per beat: The conventional EF calculation is correct, but 55 mL is the measured forward volume; regurgitant volume is the total 100 mL minus that forward component.

LV EF is about 50%, and regurgitant volume is 100 mL per beat: Neither quantity follows the given definitions: EF uses the 100 mL volume difference divided by 150 mL, and not all LV ejection is regurgitant.

questions.question: Two patients have similar stroke volume and heart rate. In an idealized arterial model, one has substantially lower large-artery compliance. Which pressure change is expected?
options: An unchanged pulse pressure because stroke volume is the same
A smaller pulse pressure because arterial storage is reduced
A larger pulse pressure for the same ejected volume
A larger pulse pressure only if cardiac output also increases
questions.explanation:
Arterial Compliance and Pulse Pressure

Correct answer: A larger pulse pressure for the same ejected volume

Relate Pulsatile Pressure to Volume Storage

**Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic arterial pressure.** In a simplified model, it increases with stroke volume and decreases with arterial compliance.

The approximation pulse pressure ≈ stroke volume/compliance explains why a stiff aorta can generate a wide pressure excursion despite an ordinary ejected volume.

Compliance is pressure dependent; the same artery can become less compliant at a higher operating pressure. Compare measurements under their actual physiologic conditions.

Avoid Treating Pulse Pressure as a Direct Flow Measurement

**The real arterial waveform also reflects ejection characteristics and wave reflection.** A peripheral cuff pressure is not interchangeable with a central aortic waveform.

A wide pulse pressure can occur with stiffness, high stroke volume or regurgitant runoff; the pressure difference alone does not identify which mechanism is present.

Likewise, a narrow pulse pressure can suggest reduced ejection but does not quantify output without assumptions about vascular properties. Interpret the finding with examination, perfusion, valve assessment and appropriate imaging. Do not infer that a higher systolic pressure necessarily means better systemic flow, or that lowering pulse pressure is itself a sufficient treatment goal. The simplified model is useful for mechanism questions while clinical decisions require the patient’s overall blood-pressure pattern, disease and treatment indications.

An unchanged pulse pressure because stroke volume is the same: Stroke volume is one determinant, but compliance also matters; equal stroke volume does not ensure equal pulse pressure in different arterial systems.

A smaller pulse pressure because arterial storage is reduced: A less compliant artery undergoes a greater pressure rise for a given volume input; reduced storage capacity does not imply a smaller pressure excursion.

A larger pulse pressure only if cardiac output also increases: Lower compliance can widen pulse pressure without an increase in stroke volume or heart rate, so a higher cardiac output is not required.

questions.question: Measured oxygen consumption is 250 mL O2/min. Arterial oxygen content is 20 mL O2/dL and mixed venous content is 15 mL O2/dL. There is no intracardiac shunt. What is cardiac output?
options: 5.0 L/min
2.5 L/min
10.0 L/min
50.0 L/min
questions.explanation:
Fick Cardiac Output and Unit Conversion

Correct answer: 5.0 L/min

Apply Conservation of Oxygen

**Cardiac output = oxygen consumption/(arterial oxygen content − mixed venous oxygen content).** The numerator and denominator must use compatible oxygen-volume units.

The content difference is 20 − 15 = 5 mL O2/dL. Dividing 250 mL O2/min by 5 mL O2/dL gives 50 dL blood/min.

Convert 50 dL/min to ==5.0 L/min==. Equivalently, convert the content difference to 50 mL O2/L before dividing.

Understand What Makes the Result Valid

**The Fick method relates tissue oxygen uptake to the difference between delivered and returning blood oxygen content.** Direct Fick uses measured oxygen consumption; assumed consumption introduces a separate source of error.

Use representative systemic arterial and mixed venous samples under sufficiently stable conditions. A central venous sample is not automatically identical to a pulmonary arterial mixed venous sample.

Intracardiac shunting requires a more careful separation of pulmonary and systemic flow and appropriate sampling. Saturation difference alone is not the same as content difference unless the hemoglobin and dissolved-oxygen assumptions are addressed. Interpret a calculated output with the measurement quality and clinical state rather than treating the arithmetic as proof that all input values are valid. A normal resting output also does not establish normal filling pressures or adequate exercise reserve.

Variable | Relationship | Units to preserve

Cardiac output | Oxygen consumption / arteriovenous content difference | mL O2/min divided by mL O2/L gives L/min

Cardiac index | CO / body surface area | L/min/m²

SVR | 80 × (MAP − RAP) / CO | dyn·s·cm⁻⁵

PVR | (mean PAP − mean PAWP) / CO | Wood units

Oxygen delivery | CO × arterial O2 content × 10 | mL O2/min when CO in L/min and content in mL/dL

questions.question: A patient has a measured cardiac output of 4.2 L/min and body surface area of 2.1 m². What is the cardiac index?
options: 2.0 L/min/m²
1.0 L/min/m²
4.2 L/min/m²
8.8 L/min/m²
questions.explanation:
Cardiac Index and Body Surface Area

Correct answer: 2.0 L/min/m²

Normalize Flow to Body Size

**Cardiac index = cardiac output/body surface area.** Substitute 4.2 L/min divided by 2.1 m² to obtain ==2.0 L/min/m²==.

Keep the indexed unit explicit. Cardiac output and cardiac index are related measurements but are not numerically interchangeable.

The same absolute output can represent a different indexed flow in two patients of different body size.

Interpret a Low Index in the Clinical State

**A low index describes reduced indexed flow, not a complete diagnosis of shock.** Assess tissue perfusion, pressure, oxygen transport and the underlying mechanism.

A low value can occur with impaired contractility, inadequate filling, excessive afterload or mechanical obstruction. Treatment selection requires distinguishing these possibilities.

Review the measurement technique and whether the patient was stable during acquisition. An assumed oxygen consumption, an unrepresentative sample or technically inconsistent thermodilution measurements can distort calculated output and therefore its index. Body-surface-area normalization also has limitations at extreme body sizes. Do not use a single index as an automatic trigger for a specific inotrope or fluid bolus. Follow the clinical trajectory and repeat appropriately acquired measurements when the result is discordant with examination, perfusion or other objective findings.

questions.question: Mean arterial pressure is 80 mmHg, mean right atrial pressure 10 mmHg and cardiac output 5 L/min. What is systemic vascular resistance in dyn·s·cm⁻⁵?
options: 1120 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵
1280 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵
1440 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵
14 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵
questions.explanation:
Systemic Vascular Resistance Calculation

Correct answer: 1120 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵

Use the Pressure Drop Across the Correct Circuit

**SVR = 80 × (MAP − mean RAP)/CO** when pressures are in mmHg and output is in L/min.

The systemic pressure gradient is 80 − 10 = 70 mmHg. Dividing by 5 L/min gives 14 mmHg·min/L, or 14 Wood units.

Multiplication by 80 gives ==1120 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵==. Omitting RAP becomes particularly misleading when venous pressure is markedly elevated.

Understand a Derived Resistance

**SVR is calculated from pressure and flow**, rather than being a direct measure of intrinsic myocardial contractility or a complete description of arterial load.

Arterial pulsatility, compliance and wave reflection also affect ventricular afterload. A single steady-flow resistance cannot capture all of those properties.

Interpret the result with the actual output and perfusion state. Identical MAP values can coexist with different combinations of cardiac output and vascular resistance. Check transducer leveling, the averaging interval and contemporaneous output acquisition when results appear inconsistent. A change in calculated resistance may reflect a change in the numerator, the denominator or both; do not infer vasoconstriction from the ratio without examining its inputs. If using cardiac index instead of output, label the result as an indexed resistance with the appropriate units.

questions.question: At right-heart catheterization, mean pulmonary artery pressure is 35 mmHg, PAWP 15 mmHg, mean right atrial pressure 10 mmHg and cardiac output 4 L/min. What is pulmonary vascular resistance?
options: 8.75 Wood units
6.25 Wood units
5.0 Wood units
0.25 Wood units
questions.explanation:
Pulmonary Vascular Resistance Calculation

Correct answer: 5.0 Wood units

Subtract the Pulmonary Downstream Pressure

**PVR = (mean PAP − PAWP)/cardiac output.** The stated transpulmonary gradient is 35 − 15 = 20 mmHg.

Divide 20 mmHg by 4 L/min to obtain ==5.0 Wood units==. If cgs units are requested, multiply by 80 to obtain 400 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵.

Right atrial pressure is not the downstream pressure for this vascular bed. It belongs in the systemic resistance calculation when subtracted from MAP.

Verify the Inputs Before Classifying Disease

**An inaccurate wedge or output produces an inaccurate resistance.** Confirm a genuine wedge recording and use an appropriate flow measurement.

A high pulmonary arterial pressure alone does not establish increased pulmonary vascular resistance; high flow and elevated left-sided filling pressure are alternative contributors.

The 2022 ESC/ERS hemodynamic classification integrates mean PAP, PAWP and PVR. A precapillary hemodynamic pattern is not itself a complete etiologic diagnosis of pulmonary arterial hypertension. Interpret values obtained during unstable physiology or major intrathoracic-pressure changes carefully. In shunt disease, pulmonary and systemic flows can differ, so the correct flow for the relevant circuit matters. These considerations make the subtraction and units necessary but not sufficient for a valid clinical conclusion.

questions.question: Hemoglobin is 8 g/dL, arterial oxygen saturation 100% and PaO2 100 mmHg. Using oxygen-binding capacity 1.34 mL/g and dissolved coefficient 0.003 mL/dL/mmHg, what is arterial oxygen content?
options: Approximately 11.0 mL O2/dL
Approximately 8.0 mL O2/dL
Approximately 13.4 mL O2/dL
Approximately 20.0 mL O2/dL
questions.explanation:
Arterial Oxygen Content in Anemia

Correct answer: Approximately 11.0 mL O2/dL

Add Bound and Dissolved Oxygen

**CaO2 = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2**, with saturation entered as a fraction and the stated units.

Hemoglobin-bound oxygen is 1.34 × 8 × 1.00 = 10.72 mL/dL. Dissolved oxygen is 0.003 × 100 = 0.30 mL/dL.

Total content is ==11.02 mL O2/dL==, approximately 11.0. Entering saturation as 100 rather than 1.00 produces a hundredfold error in the bound term.

Separate Saturation From Delivery

**A normal saturation describes the proportion of available hemoglobin binding sites occupied**, not the total amount of oxygen carried in a given volume of blood.

Anemia can therefore reduce content despite a normal PaO2 and saturation. Increasing inspired oxygen after hemoglobin is saturated mainly affects the smaller dissolved component under ordinary conditions.

Systemic oxygen delivery also depends on cardiac output: multiplying output in L/min by content in mL/dL requires a factor of ten to obtain mL O2/min. These calculations explain physiology but do not independently set a transfusion threshold. Treatment depends on bleeding, ischemia, symptoms, hemodynamics and the relevant clinical evidence. Consider dyshemoglobinemia and the measurement method when pulse oximetry, blood gas values and clinical findings disagree.

questions.question: During monitored care, true mixed venous oxygen saturation falls from 72% to 52%. Arterial saturation, hemoglobin and measured cardiac output are unchanged; the patient has developed shivering and fever. Which mechanism best explains the change?
options: Reduced systemic oxygen delivery caused by lower cardiac output
Reduced arterial oxygen content caused by desaturation
Increased oxygen consumption with greater tissue extraction
Impaired tissue oxygen extraction with venous hyperoxia
questions.explanation:
Mixed Venous Saturation and Oxygen Extraction

Correct answer: Increased oxygen consumption with greater tissue extraction

Interpret the Supply–Demand Balance

**Mixed venous saturation reflects the interaction of oxygen delivery and consumption.** When output and arterial content remain stable, greater consumption lowers returning oxygen content.

Shivering and fever can increase metabolic demand. The stated fall is therefore consistent with greater extraction rather than proving new pump failure.

A low value can also occur with anemia, hypoxemia or reduced output in other settings; those alternatives must be checked rather than inferred from saturation alone.

Check the Sample and the Clinical Context

**True mixed venous blood is sampled in the pulmonary artery after venous return has mixed.** Central venous saturation is a related but nonidentical measurement.

Sampling location, catheter position, timing and shunts can affect interpretation. Compare equivalent measurements obtained under stable acquisition conditions.

A high or normal value does not exclude shock, impaired extraction or regional tissue hypoxia. Integrate perfusion findings, lactate trends, hemoglobin, arterial oxygenation and measured flow. Treat the actual contributor rather than pursuing an isolated saturation target with empiric fluid, transfusion or inotrope therapy. When the result conflicts with the patient’s condition, verify sampling and inputs before escalating treatment. Reassessment after controlling shivering can help establish whether the proposed metabolic explanation fits the observed trajectory.

Reduced systemic oxygen delivery caused by lower cardiac output: A falling output can lower SvO2 through increased extraction, but measured output and arterial content are unchanged in this scenario.

Reduced arterial oxygen content caused by desaturation: Arterial desaturation lowers delivery and can lower SvO2, but the stem explicitly holds arterial saturation and hemoglobin unchanged.

Impaired tissue oxygen extraction with venous hyperoxia: Impaired extraction can produce a relatively high venous saturation despite tissue dysfunction; it does not explain this falling value during increased metabolic demand.

questions.question: An obese patient undergoing advanced heart-failure assessment has an indirect Fick output substantially higher than reproducible thermodilution measurements. Oxygen consumption was assumed from a formula. No shunt is identified. Which next approach best addresses the discrepancy?
options: Use the mean of the two reported outputs for derived resistance
Recalculate indirect Fick with a different estimated-consumption equation
Repeat thermodilution until a value matches the indirect Fick result
Review acquisition and, if needed, measure oxygen consumption for direct Fick
questions.explanation:
Discordant Cardiac Output Measurements

Correct answer: Review acquisition and, if needed, measure oxygen consumption for direct Fick

Distinguish Direct From Indirect Fick

**Direct Fick uses measured oxygen consumption; indirect Fick substitutes an estimate.** An error in assumed consumption is transmitted to the calculated output.

Also review arterial and mixed venous sampling, hemoglobin, oxygen conditions and whether acquisition occurred in a stable state.

A method’s familiar name does not establish that its inputs were directly measured or appropriate for this patient.

Review Thermodilution Before Choosing a Result

**Check injection technique and the consistency of repeated curves.** Catheter position, timing, temperature and circulatory abnormalities can affect the measurement.

Intracardiac shunts require special consideration and can invalidate routine thermodilution interpretation. Significant tricuspid regurgitation may also complicate assessment; avoid assuming one method is universally superior in every context.

When a difference will change pulmonary resistance, advanced-therapy eligibility or treatment, resolve it rather than hiding it in an average. State which method supplied the final output and why it was selected. Recalculate derived resistances using the chosen validated flow. Agreement with an expected clinical label is not an adequate reason to prefer a number; use technical evidence and physiologic plausibility, then document residual uncertainty if it cannot be eliminated.

Use the mean of the two reported outputs for derived resistance: Averaging potentially biased methods does not identify a valid flow and can produce an unjustified resistance estimate when the discrepancy affects a major decision.

Recalculate indirect Fick with a different estimated-consumption equation: Alternative prediction equations can change the estimate but do not establish the true individual consumption; important discordance may require direct measurement and technical review.

Repeat thermodilution until a value matches the indirect Fick result: Repeating valid acquisitions may help, but selecting only a matching value introduces bias; reproducibility and curve quality should guide acceptance rather than agreement with a preferred result.

questions.question: During supine diagnostic RHC, the transducer has been zeroed to air but is positioned well below the mid-thoracic reference level. Which correction is appropriate before interpreting filling pressures?
options: Retain the transducer position and subtract right atrial pressure from every recorded pressure
Relevel the transducer to the appropriate mid-thoracic reference and acquire respiratory-timed tracings
Rezero to air without changing the transducer height
Use the monitor’s whole-recording pressure average without releveling
questions.explanation:
Pressure Transducer Level and Respiratory Timing

Correct answer: Relevel the transducer to the appropriate mid-thoracic reference and acquire respiratory-timed tracings

Separate Leveling From Zeroing

**Zeroing and leveling are distinct steps.** The supine mid-thoracic reference approximates the left atrial level; a transducer positioned too low overreads pressure.

A transducer positioned too high underreads pressure. Changes in patient position require reassessment of the reference rather than assuming a previously correct setup remains valid.

Record the patient’s position and acquisition method so serial results can be compared meaningfully.

Interpret Respiratory Effects Explicitly

**Acquire end-expiratory pressures without a breath-holding or Valsalva maneuver in the usual diagnostic framework.** Inspect the waveform rather than relying solely on a displayed number.

Large respiratory swings, obesity, obstructive lung disease and positive-pressure ventilation require careful interpretation of intrathoracic pressure and the applicable protocol.

Respiratory timing and cardiac-cycle timing address different questions. Mean atrial pressure and an end-diastolic pressure estimate may differ, particularly with large waves or arrhythmia. Document which quantity is reported rather than silently substituting one for another. A technically small pressure error can alter classification near a diagnostic cutoff, so resolve acquisition problems before diagnosing a disease or escalating therapy from an isolated borderline result.

Retain the transducer position and subtract right atrial pressure from every recorded pressure: Pressure differences may cancel a shared offset for some calculations, but this does not validate absolute filling pressures or justify retaining an incorrect reference level.

Rezero to air without changing the transducer height: Zeroing addresses the atmospheric reference, whereas leveling addresses the hydrostatic relationship to the heart; repeating only the former does not correct the stated height error.

Use the monitor’s whole-recording pressure average without releveling: An automated average neither removes hydrostatic offset nor necessarily handles respiration and ectopy appropriately; inspect valid leveled waveforms before interpretation.

questions.question: A purported wedge tracing retains a pulmonary arterial contour. Blood aspirated in that position has saturation 70%, while systemic arterial saturation is 97%. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Classify pulmonary hypertension using the recorded wedge and calculated PVR
Accept the pressure because the balloon is inflated to the expected volume
Use pulmonary artery diastolic pressure as an equivalent substitute
Reassess catheter position and occlusion, obtain a valid wedge tracing and repeat the confirmatory sample
questions.explanation:
Confirming a Genuine Pulmonary Arterial Wedge

Correct answer: Reassess catheter position and occlusion, obtain a valid wedge tracing and repeat the confirmatory sample

Combine Waveform and Occlusion Evidence

**A genuine wedge should show an appropriate downstream atrial waveform rather than a retained PA contour.** A confirmatory aspirate should approach systemic arterial saturation when pulmonary oxygenation is normal.

In this normoxemic patient, 70% is inconsistent with the expected arterialized sample and supports further assessment rather than acceptance.

Use the appropriate careful sampling technique. Do not force an injection or aggressively manipulate an inflated balloon to obtain a desired number.

Resolve Technical Doubt Before Clinical Classification

**Repeat positioning and review waveform quality, respiratory timing and the sample conditions.** Document uncertainty if a valid wedge cannot be obtained.

Alternative assessment, including LV pressure measurement when justified, may help answer the clinical question, but LVEDP and mean PAWP are not interchangeable in every condition.

Interpret saturation confirmation alongside the full acquisition, especially with hypoxemia or unusual pulmonary venous physiology. A numerical cutoff cannot replace correct technique. Recalculate PVR after establishing the appropriate downstream pressure and output. Avoid labeling a patient with precapillary or postcapillary disease solely because an unreliable number falls on one side of a threshold; the consequences of that error extend to treatment selection and advanced-therapy assessment.

Classify pulmonary hypertension using the recorded wedge and calculated PVR: Classification and resistance depend on a valid downstream pressure; using a questionable wedge can misclassify disease and distort treatment decisions.

Accept the pressure because the balloon is inflated to the expected volume: Expected balloon volume does not establish complete occlusion; the retained PA contour and venous-like saturation suggest an inadequate wedge position.

Use pulmonary artery diastolic pressure as an equivalent substitute: PADP may approximate wedge pressure in selected circumstances, but pulmonary vascular disease can separate them; substituting it does not confirm the questioned measurement.

Confirming a Genuine Pulmonary Arterial Wedge

Correct answer: D — Reassess catheter position and occlusion, obtain a valid wedge tracing and repeat the confirmatory sample

Combine Waveform and Occlusion Evidence

  • A genuine wedge should show an appropriate downstream atrial waveform rather than a retained PA contour. A confirmatory aspirate should approach systemic arterial saturation when pulmonary oxygenation is normal.
    • In this normoxemic patient, 70% is inconsistent with the expected arterialized sample and supports further assessment rather than acceptance.
    • Use the appropriate careful sampling technique. Do not force an injection or aggressively manipulate an inflated balloon to obtain a desired number.

Resolve Technical Doubt Before Clinical Classification

  • Repeat positioning and review waveform quality, respiratory timing and the sample conditions. Document uncertainty if a valid wedge cannot be obtained.
    • Alternative assessment, including LV pressure measurement when justified, may help answer the clinical question, but LVEDP and mean PAWP are not interchangeable in every condition.
    • Interpret saturation confirmation alongside the full acquisition, especially with hypoxemia or unusual pulmonary venous physiology. A numerical cutoff cannot replace correct technique. Recalculate PVR after establishing the appropriate downstream pressure and output. Avoid labeling a patient with precapillary or postcapillary disease solely because an unreliable number falls on one side of a threshold; the consequences of that error extend to treatment selection and advanced-therapy assessment.

questions.question: A technically valid wedge tracing has large systolic v waves. High-quality valve imaging shows only mild MR, and the patient has substantial left atrial stiffness. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The pressure tracing establishes severe MR despite the imaging findings
Low left atrial compliance can generate large v waves without severe MR
A large v wave establishes primary pulmonary arterial disease
Large v waves demonstrate vigorous left atrial contraction
questions.explanation:
Large Wedge v Waves Are Not Specific for Mitral Regurgitation

Correct answer: Low left atrial compliance can generate large v waves without severe MR

Relate Pressure to Atrial Volume Accommodation

**A stiff left atrium can develop a large systolic pressure rise during filling.** Regurgitant inflow is one possible contributor to a large v wave, not its only cause.

Conversely, a compliant enlarged atrium may accommodate substantial regurgitant volume with a less dramatic pressure wave.

The waveform therefore cannot independently grade MR severity. Integrate imaging, anatomy, loading and the quality of the pressure acquisition.

Distinguish Mean Atrial Pressure From End-Diastolic Pressure

**Large v waves can raise mean PAWP above an end-diastolic pressure estimate.** Specify which quantity is being interpreted.

Mean PAWP captures the pulmonary venous/atrial pressure burden and is used in PVR calculation; an end-diastolic measurement addresses a different comparison with LVEDP.

Review discordance rather than choosing whichever pressure supports a preferred diagnosis. A valid atrial waveform may contain important physiology even when it does not match a simplistic valve label. If valve imaging is inadequate or acute MR remains clinically plausible, obtain appropriate additional imaging; that is different from declaring severe regurgitation from a tall wave alone. Reassess loading conditions and rhythm when comparing recordings obtained at different times.

The pressure tracing establishes severe MR despite the imaging findings: Large v waves are compatible with MR, but are not sufficiently specific to override adequate valve assessment; atrial compliance also determines the pressure rise during filling.

A large v wave establishes primary pulmonary arterial disease: Primary pulmonary vascular resistance does not directly define the atrial systolic filling wave; the valid wedge and atrial stiffness point to downstream pressure behavior.

Large v waves demonstrate vigorous left atrial contraction: Atrial contraction produces the a wave; the v wave reflects atrial filling during ventricular systole rather than active atrial contraction.

questions.question: A patient with substantial pulmonary vascular disease has pulmonary artery pressure 75/30 mmHg and a technically confirmed mean PAWP of 10 mmHg. Which value should supply the downstream pressure for PVR calculation?
options: The confirmed mean PAWP of 10 mmHg
The pulmonary artery diastolic pressure of 30 mmHg
The average of PADP and PAWP, 20 mmHg
The right atrial pressure measured during the same study
questions.explanation:
Pulmonary Artery Diastolic Pressure Is Not Always Wedge Pressure

Correct answer: The confirmed mean PAWP of 10 mmHg

Keep the Pulmonary Vascular Compartments Distinct

**PADP is measured upstream in the pulmonary artery; PAWP estimates downstream pressure under appropriate occlusion conditions.** They may be close when resistance is low but are not interchangeable.

A substantial separation can occur with pulmonary vascular disease. Using PADP instead of the valid wedge would erase part of the relevant pressure gradient.

PVR uses mean PAP minus mean PAWP divided by the appropriate cardiac output. Do not substitute a systolic or diastolic PA pressure for the mean in that formula.

Resolve a Questioned Wedge by Verification

**If a wedge appears implausible, confirm its acquisition rather than automatically replacing it with PADP.** Review contour, respiratory timing, level and occlusion evidence.

This stem explicitly supplies a technically confirmed wedge, so there is no basis for replacing it with a numerically higher pressure simply because pulmonary arterial pressure is high.

The diastolic pulmonary gradient and PVR describe related but different aspects of physiology. Contemporary disease classification should use the specified guideline framework rather than an isolated surrogate. A pressure discrepancy is information to interpret, not an error to eliminate by averaging. Document the original measured values and the reasoning behind derived calculations so that classification and subsequent treatment decisions remain traceable to valid inputs.

The pulmonary artery diastolic pressure of 30 mmHg: PADP can approximate wedge pressure under suitable pulmonary vascular conditions, but the approximation fails with a substantial pulmonary vascular gradient as in this patient.

The average of PADP and PAWP, 20 mmHg: Averaging measurements of different physiologic compartments does not create a validated downstream pressure and would underestimate the transpulmonary gradient here.

The right atrial pressure measured during the same study: RAP is the downstream pressure used for systemic vascular resistance, not the pulmonary venous/left atrial pressure estimate required for PVR.

questions.question: Which resting hemodynamic combination meets the 2022 ESC/ERS definition of precapillary pulmonary hypertension?
options: Mean PAP 23 mmHg, PAWP 12 mmHg and PVR 2.0 Wood units
Mean PAP 20 mmHg, PAWP 12 mmHg and PVR 2.5 Wood units
Mean PAP 23 mmHg, PAWP 17 mmHg and PVR 2.5 Wood units
Mean PAP 23 mmHg, PAWP 12 mmHg and PVR 2.5 Wood units
questions.explanation:
Precapillary Pulmonary Hypertension: Contemporary Thresholds

Correct answer: Mean PAP 23 mmHg, PAWP 12 mmHg and PVR 2.5 Wood units

Apply All Three Conditions

**The 2022 ESC/ERS resting precapillary definition requires mean PAP above 20 mmHg, PAWP at or below 15 mmHg and PVR above 2 Wood units.** Each boundary matters.

A pressure of 20 is not above 20, and a resistance of 2 is not above 2. The proposed correct combination satisfies all three conditions.

The lower contemporary thresholds should not be replaced by the older mean PAP threshold of 25 or an older PVR threshold when the question explicitly names this framework.

Separate a Hemodynamic Pattern From Etiology

**Precapillary PH is not synonymous with group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension.** Lung disease, chronic thromboembolic disease and other causes require assessment.

Use validated invasive measurements and the clinical investigation pathway to establish the cause. Echo estimates alone do not provide the same three-variable invasive classification.

A revised diagnostic boundary does not mean every patient near the new threshold has established benefit from the same drug regimen used in older trials. Review symptoms, risk factors, imaging and the quality of the wedge and output measurements before treatment decisions. Borderline findings may need further context or reassessment; the classification is a starting point for causal evaluation rather than permission to assign a specific pulmonary vasodilator.

Mean PAP 23 mmHg, PAWP 12 mmHg and PVR 2.0 Wood units: The precapillary definition requires PVR greater than 2; with low wedge and PVR at or below 2, elevated mean pressure may represent an unclassified hemodynamic pattern.

Mean PAP 20 mmHg, PAWP 12 mmHg and PVR 2.5 Wood units: The definition requires mean PAP greater than 20, so a value exactly 20 does not meet the resting PH threshold despite the elevated resistance.

Mean PAP 23 mmHg, PAWP 17 mmHg and PVR 2.5 Wood units: The wedge is above 15 and therefore indicates a postcapillary component; with PVR above 2 this is a combined pattern rather than purely precapillary PH.

questions.question: A stable patient has mean PAP 32 mmHg, mean PAWP 20 mmHg and cardiac output 4 L/min. The measurements are technically valid. Under 2022 ESC/ERS definitions, which pattern is present?
options: Isolated postcapillary pulmonary hypertension
Combined post- and precapillary pulmonary hypertension
Precapillary pulmonary hypertension without a postcapillary component
Unclassified pulmonary hypertension with low resistance
questions.explanation:
Combined Post- and Precapillary Pulmonary Hypertension

Correct answer: Combined post- and precapillary pulmonary hypertension

Calculate Resistance Before Assigning the Pattern

**The transpulmonary gradient is 32 − 20 = 12 mmHg and PVR is 12/4 = 3 Wood units.** Mean PAP and PAWP are elevated.

With mean PAP above 20, PAWP above 15 and PVR above 2, the pattern is combined post- and precapillary PH.

If PVR were at or below 2 with the same elevated mean PAP and wedge, the hemodynamic label would be isolated postcapillary PH.

Do Not Turn the Label Into an Automatic Drug Choice

**A combined pattern identifies increased resistance in addition to elevated downstream pressure.** It does not itself establish group 1 PAH or an indication for a PAH-specific drug.

Evaluate the left-heart substrate, volume state, valve disease and other contributors. Confirm that pressure and flow values were acquired under comparable stable conditions.

A large v wave, an incorrect wedge or an inaccurate output can alter the derived resistance. Use mean PAWP for the resistance calculation rather than substituting an end-diastolic value without explaining the purpose. Management follows the underlying disease and applicable evidence. Repeating or extending assessment is preferable to treating a technically questionable boundary value as a definitive etiologic diagnosis.

Pattern with mean PAP >20 mmHg | PAWP | PVR

Precapillary | ≤15 mmHg | >2 WU

Isolated postcapillary | >15 mmHg | ≤2 WU

Combined post- and precapillary | >15 mmHg | >2 WU

Unclassified low-resistance pattern | ≤15 mmHg | ≤2 WU

Isolated postcapillary pulmonary hypertension: The elevated wedge establishes a postcapillary component, but PVR is (32-20)/4 = 3 WU, exceeding the 2-WU boundary for an isolated postcapillary pattern.

Precapillary pulmonary hypertension without a postcapillary component: The wedge is above 15 mmHg, so the case does not meet the low-wedge requirement for a purely precapillary classification.

Unclassified pulmonary hypertension with low resistance: That category can apply to elevated mean PAP with PAWP at or below 15 and PVR at or below 2; neither the wedge nor resistance in this patient fits it.

questions.question: A patient with unexplained systemic venous congestion undergoes simultaneous LV and RV pressure recording during spontaneous breathing. With inspiration, RV systolic pressure rises while LV systolic pressure falls. Which diagnosis is most strongly supported by this dynamic finding?
options: Isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension
Restrictive cardiomyopathy
Constrictive pericarditis
Severe tricuspid regurgitation
questions.explanation:
Respiratory Ventricular Discordance in Constriction

Correct answer: Constrictive pericarditis

Use Dynamic Interaction Rather Than a Static Contour Alone

**Constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence and limits transmission of intrathoracic pressure to the cardiac chambers.** Inspiration favors RV filling at the expense of LV filling.

Simultaneous recordings can therefore show reciprocal respiratory changes in ventricular systolic pressures. Compare equivalent beats and identify the respiratory phase directly.

Equalized diastolic pressures or a dip-and-plateau pattern are less specific and can also occur with restrictive physiology.

Integrate Invasive and Imaging Evidence

**Use echo and CT or CMR to evaluate physiology and the pericardium.** A normal pericardial thickness does not exclude constriction.

Respiratory septal shift, tissue-Doppler behavior and hepatic venous flow can contribute to the assessment; no single anatomic or pressure finding should replace the integrated diagnosis.

Rhythm irregularity, loading conditions and ventilation can complicate interpretation, and mixed myocardial–pericardial disease may occur. Establish the cause and whether inflammation or chronic fixed constriction is present before selecting therapy. The diagnostic value here arises from the simultaneous dynamic behavior, not simply the fact that both filling pressures are high. Document acquisition conditions so a later reviewer can verify that apparent discordance was not created by comparing unrelated beats or separate respiratory cycles.

Isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension: Pulmonary vascular disease can elevate RV pressure, but an elevated right-sided pressure alone does not explain the characteristic reciprocal LV/RV respiratory coupling.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Restriction can produce high filling pressures and a dip-and-plateau contour, but usually preserves concordant respiratory ventricular pressure changes rather than the stated reciprocal behavior.

Severe tricuspid regurgitation: TR can cause venous congestion and large right atrial systolic waves, but does not by itself establish the demonstrated dynamic biventricular pressure discordance.

    • Simultaneous recordings can therefore show reciprocal respiratory changes in ventricular systolic pressures. Compare equivalent beats and identify the respiratory phase directly.
    • Equalized diastolic pressures or a dip-and-plateau pattern are less specific and can also occur with restrictive physiology.

Integrate Invasive and Imaging Evidence

  • Use echo and CT or CMR to evaluate physiology and the pericardium. A normal pericardial thickness does not exclude constriction.
    • Respiratory septal shift, tissue-Doppler behavior and hepatic venous flow can contribute to the assessment; no single anatomic or pressure finding should replace the integrated diagnosis.
    • Rhythm irregularity, loading conditions and ventilation can complicate interpretation, and mixed myocardial–pericardial disease may occur. Establish the cause and whether inflammation or chronic fixed constriction is present before selecting therapy. The diagnostic value here arises from the simultaneous dynamic behavior, not simply the fact that both filling pressures are high. Document acquisition conditions so a later reviewer can verify that apparent discordance was not created by comparing unrelated beats or separate respiratory cycles.

Other Options

  • A — Isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension: Pulmonary vascular disease can elevate RV pressure, but an elevated right-sided pressure alone does not explain the characteristic reciprocal LV/RV respiratory coupling.
  • B — Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Restriction can produce high filling pressures and a dip-and-plateau contour, but usually preserves concordant respiratory ventricular pressure changes rather than the stated reciprocal behavior.
  • D — Severe tricuspid regurgitation: TR can cause venous congestion and large right atrial systolic waves, but does not by itself establish the demonstrated dynamic biventricular pressure discordance.

questions.question: A patient with suspected important mitral leaflet pathology has a technically inadequate TTE despite optimization. Detailed leaflet anatomy will change an imminent repair decision. There is no relevant esophageal contraindication. Which next test most directly addresses the question?
options: CMR focused on regurgitant volume and ventricular remodeling
Ultrasound-enhanced transthoracic imaging focused on LV cavity definition
Transesophageal echocardiography
Cardiac CT focused on mitral annular geometry and calcification
questions.explanation:
Selecting TEE After a Nondiagnostic Transthoracic Study

Correct answer: Transesophageal echocardiography

Match the Test to the Unresolved Anatomy

**TEE can provide high-resolution imaging of posterior cardiac structures and detailed mitral anatomy**, particularly when transthoracic windows are inadequate.

The value lies in answering a management-relevant question, not simply obtaining an additional test. TTE remains the usual initial study for many structural assessments.

Three-dimensional TEE can clarify the affected leaflet segments and mechanism when available and technically adequate.

Plan a Safe and Useful Examination

**Assess esophageal history, airway and sedation risks before proceeding.** A technically attractive modality may be unsuitable when procedural risk is unacceptable.

Esophageal obstruction, perforation or other important pathology requires an appropriate alternative assessment and specialist risk evaluation. Monitoring and preparation follow the procedural protocol.

Interpret valve severity under the acquisition’s loading conditions, since sedation and changes in blood pressure can alter regurgitation. TEE anatomy and Doppler findings complement rather than erase a valid earlier assessment. If the study will not change a decision or the question is already answered by adequate TTE, its added invasiveness may not be justified. Explain the specific purpose and use the resulting mechanism assessment to inform the multidisciplinary intervention plan.

TEE | Detailed mitral mechanism and procedural anatomy | Esophageal and sedation risks

CMR | Regurgitant flow and ventricular volumes | Safety, artifact and acquisition feasibility

Cardiac CT | Annular geometry and calcification | Contrast, radiation and motion considerations

Ultrasound-enhanced transthoracic imaging focused on LV cavity definition: An enhancing agent can improve endocardial border definition and selected Doppler signals, but does not necessarily overcome the inadequate detailed leaflet imaging needed for repair planning.

Cardiac CT focused on mitral annular geometry and calcification: CT is useful for annular anatomy and procedural planning, but the immediate question of detailed leaflet pathology after inadequate TTE is most directly addressed by TEE.

questions.question: Continuous-wave Doppler records a peak velocity of 4.0 m/s across a stenotic valve. Proximal velocity is negligible. Using the simplified Bernoulli equation, what is the peak instantaneous pressure gradient?
options: 64 mmHg
16 mmHg
32 mmHg
80 mmHg
questions.explanation:
Doppler Peak Instantaneous Pressure Gradient

Correct answer: 64 mmHg

Square the Velocity Before Multiplication

**Peak instantaneous gradient = 4 × Vmax²**, with velocity in m/s and gradient in mmHg under the usual simplified assumptions.

Substitute 4 × (4.0)² = 4 × 16 = ==64 mmHg==. The velocity must be squared; an error in measured velocity is therefore amplified.

This calculation estimates the pressure difference at the instant of peak velocity, not an average over systole.

Keep Different Gradients Distinct

**Mean Doppler gradient is obtained by averaging instantaneous gradients through the ejection period.** It is not four times the square of an arithmetic mean velocity.

A catheter peak-to-peak gradient compares pressure peaks that occur at different times and is not interchangeable with a Doppler peak instantaneous gradient.

The simplified equation neglects proximal velocity; when it is substantial, the fuller velocity-difference relationship may be needed. Doppler alignment matters because an oblique beam underestimates velocity. Pressure recovery, flow state and serial obstructions can also complicate comparison with invasive data. Do not grade a valve or decide on intervention from this isolated arithmetic result: integrate valve area, mean gradient, flow, anatomy and symptoms. State the type of gradient in the report so the number is not later misread as an invasive or mean measurement.

ASE recommendations for Doppler echocardiographic quantification — https://anesthesia.bidmc.harvard.edu/ADEL/documents/echo/ASE%20Recommendations%20for%20Quantification%20of%20Doppler%20Echo%202001.pdf

questions.question: LVOT diameter is 2.0 cm and the correctly acquired pulsed-wave LVOT VTI is 20 cm. Assuming a circular LVOT, what is Doppler stroke volume?
options: Approximately 126 mL
Approximately 31 mL
Approximately 80 mL
Approximately 63 mL
questions.explanation:
LVOT Doppler Stroke Volume

Correct answer: Approximately 63 mL

Multiply Cross-Sectional Area by Flow Distance

**Stroke volume = LVOT area × LVOT VTI.** With a circular assumption, area = πd²/4 = 0.785 × d².

For d = 2.0 cm, area is 0.785 × 4 = 3.14 cm². Multiply by VTI 20 cm to obtain 62.8 cm³, or ==approximately 63 mL==.

VTI is a distance traveled during one beat, not peak velocity and not a minute-volume measurement.

Preserve Measurement Consistency

**Use diameter and Doppler sampling that refer to the appropriate corresponding outflow location.** Diameter error is squared in the area calculation.

Sample placement in accelerated flow or Doppler misalignment can bias the result. Irregular rhythm requires appropriate beat selection and averaging rather than mixing incompatible cycles.

Cardiac output would require multiplication by heart rate and conversion from mL to L. This forward outflow measurement is not necessarily total LV ejection when regurgitation is present; aortic regurgitation also separates antegrade systolic flow from net systemic flow. Interpret changes using comparable technique and loading conditions. A plausible numerical result does not validate an inadequately visualized diameter or a poorly acquired envelope, so review the original images when the derived stroke volume conflicts with the clinical picture.

questions.question: An LVOT diameter of 2.0 cm is entered as 1.8 cm. All VTIs are unchanged. By approximately what percentage are the calculated LVOT stroke volume and continuity-equation aortic valve area underestimated?
questions.explanation:
Squared Diameter Error in LVOT Calculations

Correct answer: 19%

Calculate the Ratio Before the Percentage

**Area is proportional to diameter squared.** The entered-to-true area ratio is 1.8²/2.0² = 3.24/4.00 = 0.81.

Calculated area is therefore 81% of the true value, an ==underestimate of 19%==. At unchanged VTI, LVOT stroke volume has the same proportional error.

Continuity-equation valve area also scales with LVOT area when both relevant VTIs remain unchanged, so its calculated value is underestimated by the same percentage.

Review the Source of Discordant Valve Measurements

**A small diameter error can materially change a derived valve area.** The flow velocity and gradient may remain unchanged while the calculated area appears smaller.

Inspect the original diameter, sampling site, geometric assumption and Doppler envelopes before interpreting discordant stenosis severity.

The approximate small-error rule doubles the fractional diameter error, but the exact squared ratio gives 19% rather than 20% here. A noncircular outflow tract introduces another limitation of a single two-dimensional diameter. Do not correct a suspected error by choosing a diameter that produces an expected valve area; reacquire or independently verify the measurement. Clinical decisions integrate symptoms, flow and other valid severity measures, with additional imaging when appropriate. Preserve the raw measurements so a reviewer can distinguish a genuine physiologic discrepancy from a calculation or acquisition problem.

questions.question: Serial studies show GLS changing from −20% to −16%, while EF remains similar. The second examination was acquired during marked hypertension using different analysis software. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Improved longitudinal shortening with stable global chamber emptying
Reduced shortening magnitude requiring review of loading and method comparability
New intrinsic systolic dysfunction requiring treatment escalation from this comparison
Measurement variation that can be set aside because EF is stable
questions.explanation:
Strain Changes and Loading Conditions

Correct answer: Reduced shortening magnitude requiring review of loading and method comparability

Interpret the Sign and Magnitude

**Longitudinal shortening is conventionally expressed as negative strain.** A change from −20% to −16% is a reduction in absolute shortening magnitude.

EF and GLS describe different aspects of chamber behavior and need not change in parallel. A preserved EF does not establish normal longitudinal mechanics.

Numerical interpretation precedes disease attribution: recognizing a worse value does not establish why it changed.

Assess Serial Comparability

**Blood pressure, loading, rhythm, image quality and analysis method can influence strain.** Use comparable acquisition and software where possible.

Review tracking, region-of-interest placement, frame quality and timing before diagnosing progression from a serial difference.

Repeat or corroborate a clinically important finding under appropriate conditions and integrate symptoms, biomarkers and the disease-specific context. Avoid applying a universal diagnostic cutoff to every vendor, age group or clinical indication. A relative change may have a defined role in a particular surveillance protocol, but that protocol’s assumptions and baseline quality remain necessary. This patient’s hypertension and changed software create identifiable alternative explanations that must be addressed before assigning new myocardial injury or changing treatment on the strain value alone.

Improved longitudinal shortening with stable global chamber emptying: A change from −20 to −16 is less negative and therefore represents reduced shortening magnitude; the numerical sign should not be mistaken for improvement.

New intrinsic systolic dysfunction requiring treatment escalation from this comparison: The change may be important, but hypertension and changed software are material alternative explanations; confirm comparability before attributing it to intrinsic deterioration.

Measurement variation that can be set aside because EF is stable: Stable EF does not invalidate a strain change, which can reveal different functional information; review acquisition and context rather than dismissing it.

questions.question: A symptomatic patient in sinus rhythm has transmitral E/A of 1.1. Mitral annular relaxation velocities are reduced and other measurements raise concern for elevated filling pressure. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Normal relaxation with a high-normal filling pressure
Possible pseudonormal inflow requiring integrated pressure assessment
Impaired relaxation with normal filling pressure established by E/A
Restrictive filling established by the near-one E/A ratio
questions.explanation:
A Normal-Appearing E/A Ratio Does Not Exclude Raised Filling Pressure

Correct answer: Possible pseudonormal inflow requiring integrated pressure assessment

Understand Pseudonormal Filling

**Transmitral E and A velocities reflect pressure gradients as well as relaxation.** Increased atrial pressure can augment early filling despite impaired myocardial relaxation.

The resulting E/A ratio can resemble a normal pattern. Age, heart rate, atrial function and loading further influence the ratio.

Use a multiparameter assessment rather than assigning normal function from the apparent inflow balance.

Separate Relaxation From Pressure Estimation

**Tissue Doppler e′ helps assess relaxation, while E/e′ and other evidence contribute to pressure assessment.** Neither quantity is universally reliable in isolation.

The 2025 ASE update incorporates a structured assessment with complementary measurements and disease-specific considerations. Rhythm, valve disease and technical limitations determine which framework is applicable.

Atrial size can reflect chronic pressure burden but is affected by other conditions and does not establish the pressure at one moment. Pulmonary pressure estimates also require interpretation of the right-heart and pulmonary context. When noninvasive findings remain indeterminate and exertional symptoms persist, further appropriate functional or invasive assessment may be necessary. Diagnose a clinical HFpEF syndrome using the complete evidence, rather than equating either a normal EF or one abnormal Doppler measure with the final diagnosis.

Normal relaxation with a high-normal filling pressure: Reduced annular relaxation velocities contradict an assumption of normal relaxation; the near-one inflow ratio can be restored by increased atrial pressure.

questions.question: A patient with persistent AF has exertional dyspnea and preserved EF. The operator cannot identify a consistent transmitral A wave and obtains variable E velocities across beats. Which approach best reflects the 2025 ASE guidance?
options: An AF-specific multiparameter assessment using representative cycles
The sinus-rhythm E/A pathway using the clearest apparent late filling wave
A single-cycle septal E/e′ classification at the longest RR interval
A chronic-pressure classification based principally on LA volume
questions.explanation:
Diastolic Assessment in Atrial Fibrillation

Correct answer: An AF-specific multiparameter assessment using representative cycles

Use a Framework Appropriate to the Rhythm

**AF alters filling assessment through loss of organized atrial contraction and variable cycle length.** The sinus-rhythm E/A framework cannot simply be applied unchanged.

The 2025 ASE update provides a separate AF pathway and recommends representative measurements across several cycles. No single echo marker supplies a sufficiently strong stand-alone pressure estimate.

Select cycles that reflect the average heart rate rather than extreme intervals that generate misleadingly high or low velocities.

Combine Complementary Findings

**The AF pathway integrates inflow, annular and pulmonary-pressure information.** Additional atrial and pulmonary venous findings can help when the initial assessment is unresolved.

Acquire technically valid signals and retain an indeterminate result when information is inadequate rather than forcing a normal or elevated label.

Consider important valve disease and other disease-specific exceptions before applying an algorithm. Even a technically sound pressure estimate is one component of explaining dyspnea; assess ischemic, pulmonary and other causes according to context. If resting results do not explain symptoms, further appropriately selected testing may be needed. Document rhythm, rate and averaging so subsequent studies can be compared meaningfully rather than interpreting beat-selection differences as disease progression.

The sinus-rhythm E/A pathway using the clearest apparent late filling wave: AF lacks organized atrial contraction, so selecting a late deflection does not restore the validity of a sinus-rhythm E/A classification.

A single-cycle septal E/e′ classification at the longest RR interval: E/e′ may contribute, but one selected extreme interval can misrepresent the usual state; the guideline uses a multiparameter representative-cycle approach.

A chronic-pressure classification based principally on LA volume: Atrial enlargement may reflect AF and remodeling as well as pressure burden, so it cannot independently establish the current filling pressure in this patient.

questions.question: A patient with severe functional TR has TAPSE 2.0 cm but marked RV enlargement, abnormal free-wall strain and impaired fractional area change. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Integrated evidence of RV dysfunction despite preserved annular excursion
Preserved global RV function with isolated regional strain abnormalities
Technical strain error as the preferred explanation for all discordance
Indeterminate RV function until invasive pressures have been measured
questions.explanation:
TAPSE Does Not Fully Describe Right Ventricular Function

Correct answer: Integrated evidence of RV dysfunction despite preserved annular excursion

Recognize What TAPSE Measures

**TAPSE measures longitudinal motion of the lateral tricuspid annulus**, not the entire RV contraction pattern or effective forward output.

A value above 1.7 cm is generally within the normal range, but severe TR, loading and altered annular mechanics can produce misleading preservation.

Check alignment and image quality, then interpret excursion alongside the chamber’s size, shape and other functional measures.

Use a Comprehensive Right-Heart Assessment

**Integrate fractional area change, tissue velocities, free-wall strain and three-dimensional measures when feasible.** Each supplies complementary information.

Assess TR severity, pulmonary loading, venous congestion and forward flow. Apparent improvement in a load-sensitive index does not necessarily indicate myocardial recovery.

Use CMR or invasive assessment when a specific unresolved question will alter management, rather than treating a single discordant index as a reason to ignore the remainder of the study. Serial comparisons require similar views, technique and loading. The 2025 ASE guideline emphasizes systematic right-heart evaluation; reporting one normal-looking number without the abnormal context can obscure clinically important maladaptation and delay an appropriate valve or pulmonary vascular assessment.

Preserved global RV function with isolated regional strain abnormalities: TAPSE samples annular motion rather than global function; abnormal FAC and marked remodeling prevent concluding that global performance is preserved from this value.

Technical strain error as the preferred explanation for all discordance: Tracking error should be checked, but independent abnormal FAC and RV remodeling support a real problem; a normal-looking TAPSE does not make strain error the preferred global explanation.

Indeterminate RV function until invasive pressures have been measured: Pressures may clarify loading, but echo can identify dysfunction through multiple valid measures; invasive assessment is not required merely to recognize this pattern.
